title: Numbers to 10 000
blurb: Reading and writing four-digit numbers, place value to thousands, comparing and ordering, rounding to 10 and 100, and skip-counting patterns.

lessons.title: Reading & Writing Numbers
lessons.concreteComparison: A herder with $3\,482$ sheep cannot count them one by one at a glance — but say the number as THREE thousands, FOUR hundreds, EIGHT tens and TWO ones, and it fits in four short words. Every four-digit number is just four columns standing in a row, and each column has a name: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones.
lessons.objective: Read four-digit numerals in words and write word names as numerals, name the thousands, hundreds, tens and ones columns, and use zero to hold a column that is empty.
concept: **Four columns, four names.** A four-digit number has a thousands column, a hundreds column, a tens column and a ones column — always in that order, biggest on the left. In $3\,482$: $3$ thousands, $4$ hundreds, $8$ tens, $2$ ones.

**Reading is naming the columns.** $3\,482$ reads "three thousand four hundred and eighty-two" — the words walk the columns left to right. Writing goes the other way: hear the words, fill the columns. The little word "and" before the last part is optional: "three thousand four hundred and eighty-two" and "three thousand four hundred eighty-two" name the same number. This topic always says "and", so your answers can too.
**Zero holds an empty column.** $4\,052$ has NO hundreds — but the column cannot be left out, or the other digits would slide into the wrong places. The zero is a guard standing in the empty column.
lessons.keyIdea: Four-digit numbers are four named columns — thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. Reading walks the columns left to right, and zero stands guard in any column that is empty.

facts.title: The four columns
facts.explanation: Biggest column on the left; each digit sits in exactly one column.

facts.title: Zero stands guard
facts.explanation: An empty column keeps its zero — drop it and every other digit slides.

workedExamples.note: Walk the columns left to right.
workedExamples.solution: $3$ thousands, $4$ hundreds, $8$ tens, $2$ ones: "three thousand four hundred and eighty-two". The columns rebuild it: $3\,000 + 400 + 80 + 2 = 3\,482$.

workedExamples.statement: Write "four thousand and fifty-two" as a numeral.
workedExamples.note: No hundreds are spoken — so the hundreds column gets a zero.
workedExamples.solution: $4$ in the thousands, nothing in the hundreds, $5$ in the tens, $2$ in the ones: $4\,052$. The zero guards the empty hundreds column — without it the digits would collapse to $452$.

commonMistakes.text: Putting the fifty in the wrong column — writing "four thousand and fifty-two" as 4 520.
commonMistakes.correction: Fifty is 5 TENS. The hundreds column is empty and keeps its zero: 4 052. Adding the columns back exposes the slip — 4 000 + 500 + 20 makes 4 520, the wrong number.

commonMistakes.text: Skipping the zero when reading — calling 4 052 "four hundred and fifty-two".
commonMistakes.correction: The 4 stands in the THOUSANDS column, four places from the right. Read the columns, not just the digits: four thousand and fifty-two.

tryIt.solution: $6$ thousands, $7$ hundreds, $0$ tens, $4$ ones: "six thousand seven hundred and four". The empty tens column is silent in words but keeps its zero in the numeral.

tryIt.statement: Write "nine thousand six hundred and forty" as a numeral.
tryIt.solution: Columns: $9$, $6$, $4$, and an empty ones column — $9\,640$.

steps.title: Four columns, read left to right
beats: Every four-digit number is four columns standing in a row: THOUSANDS, HUNDREDS, TENS, ONES — biggest on the left. The place gives the digit its value.
$3\,482$ is $3$ thousands, $4$ hundreds, $8$ tens and $2$ ones — the picture below shows the four columns as four groups.
Reading just walks the columns: "three thousand four hundred and eighty-two". Writing walks back: hear the words, fill the columns.

steps.title: Numerals into words
steps.intro: Name each column, then say them left to right.

steps: "Three thousand four hundred and eighty-two" — and the columns rebuild it: $3\,000 + 400 + 80 + 2$.
examples.answer: three thousand four hundred and eighty-two
five thousand two hundred and seventeen

steps.title: Name the columns
steps.intro: Which column is each digit standing in?

problems.prompt: In $7\,368$, the digit in the hundreds column is:
problems.explanation: Count columns from the left: $7$ thousands, $3$ hundreds, $6$ tens, $8$ ones. The hundreds digit is $3$ — the $6$ is tens and the $7$ is thousands.

options: two thousand five hundred and ninety
problems.explanation: Columns: $2$ thousands, $5$ hundreds, $9$ tens, $0$ ones. "Two thousand and fifty-nine" would be $2\,059$ — it moves the $5$ out of the hundreds.

problems.prompt: Which numeral is "eight thousand three hundred and six"?
problems.explanation: Six ONES, so the $6$ ends the number and a zero guards the tens: $8\,306$. Choosing $8\,360$ puts the six in the tens — that reads "sixty".

steps.title: Find the column
steps.prompt: In $6\,437$, the digit $4$ stands in which column?
steps.explanation: Walk from the left: $6$ thousands, $4$ hundreds, $3$ tens, $7$ ones. Standing in the hundreds column, the $4$ is worth $4 \times 100 = 400$ — the place gives the digit its value.

steps.title: Nine thousand of them
steps.body: How many four-digit numbers exist? They run from $1\,000$ up to $9\,999$, so there are $9\,999 - 1\,000 + 1 = 9\,000$ of them — nine thousand numbers, and this topic's four columns can name every single one.

steps.title: Zero stands guard
beats: What if a column is EMPTY? $4\,052$ has $4$ thousands, $5$ tens, $2$ ones — and no hundreds at all. In the picture the hundreds column is still standing, holding nothing: $0$ hundreds.
The empty column still needs a digit, or everything slides: drop the zero from $4\,052$ and you get $452$ — a completely different number. Zero is the guard that keeps every other digit in its place.
Words to numerals: "three thousand and eight" has empty hundreds AND empty tens — two guards: $3\,008$.

steps.title: Words into numerals
steps.intro: Fill all four columns; empty ones get a zero.

examples.prompt: Write "four thousand and fifty-two" as a numeral.
steps: The guard goes in: $4\,052$ — not $452$, which has lost a whole column.

examples.prompt: Write "six thousand seven hundred and four" as a numeral.

steps.title: Guard duty
steps.intro: Spot the empty columns before writing.

problems.prompt: "Three thousand and eight" as a numeral is:
problems.explanation: Eight ONES and two empty columns between: $3\,008$. Writing $3\,800$ promotes the eight into the hundreds — that reads "eight hundred".

problems.prompt: In $9\,041$, the zero holds which column?
problems.explanation: Columns left to right: $9$ thousands, $0$ hundreds, $4$ tens, $1$ one. The guard stands in the hundreds.

problems.prompt: Which number has a zero in the TENS column?
problems.explanation: In $5\,306$ the columns are $5, 3, 0, 6$ — zero on tens duty. In $5\,360$ the zero guards the ones; in $5\,036$ it guards the hundreds.

steps.title: The fifth column
steps.prompt: Counting up from $9\,999$, the very next number needs:
options: no change — $9\,999$ is the last number
steps.explanation: One more than $9\,999$ is $9\,999 + 1 = 10\,000$ — ten thousand, the first number too big for four columns. This whole topic lives below it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Four columns, left to right: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones.
Reading walks the columns; writing fills them from the words.
An empty column keeps a zero — drop it and every digit slides.
The place gives the digit its value: the same 4 can mean 4, 40, 400 or 4 000.
Ten thousand is the first number that needs a fifth column.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every number below, touch each column and say its name — thousands, hundreds, tens, ones — before you answer. The naming is the method.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Both directions, guards included.

options: six thousand two hundred and thirty-five
six thousand two hundred and fifty-three
problems.explanation: Columns $6, 2, 3, 5$ — thirty-five, not fifty-three: the $3$ is tens and the $5$ is ones.
Leftmost column of a four-digit number is thousands: the $1$, worth $1\,000$. The $9$ is hundreds.

problems.prompt: "Seven thousand and ninety" as a numeral is:
problems.explanation: Ninety is $9$ TENS, so the hundreds column is empty and gets its guard: $7\,090$. Writing $7\,900$ turns ninety into nine hundred.
Two guards hold the hundreds and tens; only thousands and ones speak: "two thousand and four". "Two thousand and forty" would be $2\,040$.

problems.prompt: A herder's winter count is $5\,067$ animals. In words that is:
options: five thousand six hundred and seven
problems.explanation: Columns $5, 0, 6, 7$: the zero silences the hundreds, so the words jump from thousands straight to sixty-seven.

steps.title: You've finished "Reading & Writing Numbers"
steps.body: Four named columns and a zero standing guard — you can now read and write every number below ten thousand. Next: what each digit is WORTH, and how to take a number apart into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.

lessons.title: Place Value
lessons.concreteComparison: Pay $3\,482$ togrog at the shop: three $1\,000$ notes, four $100$ notes, eight $10$ coins and two $1$ coins. The SAME kind of counting hides inside every number — each digit is a count of notes of one size, and the column says which size. That is place value.
lessons.objective: Say what each digit of a four-digit number is worth, write numbers in expanded form, and build numbers back from thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
concept: **A digit's worth is digit times place.** In $3\,482$ the $3$ stands in the thousands column, so it is worth $3 \times 1\,000 = 3\,000$ — not $3$. Same digit in the tens column would be worth only $30$.
**Expanded form takes the number apart.** $3\,482$ $= 3\,000 + 400 + 80 + 2$: one part per column, and the parts really do add back to the number. It is the note-and-coin payment written as a sum.
**Building runs it backwards.** Given $8\,000 + 40 + 6$, fill the columns: $8$ thousands, $0$ hundreds (the guard returns), $4$ tens, $6$ ones — $8\,046$. Parts in, number out.
lessons.keyIdea: Each digit is worth digit times place: expanded form spells the worths out as a sum, and building from parts folds the sum back into a numeral — with zero guarding any missing part.

facts.title: Worth = digit × place
facts.explanation: Read the place before the digit — the column multiplies the digit.

facts.title: Expanded form
facts.explanation: One part per column; the parts add back to the number exactly.

workedExamples.statement: What is the $7$ worth in $2\,745$? And in $7\,245$?
workedExamples.note: Same digit, different column, different worth.
workedExamples.solution: In $2\,745$ the $7$ stands in the hundreds: worth $7 \times 100 = 700$. In $7\,245$ it stands in the thousands: worth $7 \times 1\,000 = 7\,000$ — ten times as much, one column over.
$3$ thousands $= 3\,000$, $4$ hundreds $= 400$, $8$ tens $= 80$, $2$ ones $= 2$. So $3\,482$ $= 3\,000 + 400 + 80 + 2$ — and the parts add straight back.

commonMistakes.correction: The digit alone is 3, but its PLACE multiplies it: 3 × 1 000 = 3 000. Cover the other digits and read what remains: 3 000.

commonMistakes.text: Expanded form that invents a part — writing 4 052 as 4 000 + 500 + 2.
commonMistakes.correction: The 5 stands in the TENS column: 4 052 = 4 000 + 50 + 2. Check by adding your parts back — 4 000 + 500 + 2 = 4 502, the wrong number.

tryIt.solution: $6\,000 + 900 + 10 + 3$ — four parts, one per column, adding back to $6\,913$.

steps.title: What each digit is worth
beats: The place gives the digit its value: a digit is worth digit TIMES place. In $2\,745$ — pictured below as notes and coins — the $2$ is worth $2\,000$, the $7$ is worth $700$, the $4$ is worth $40$, the $5$ just $5$.
Move a digit one column left and its worth grows ten times: $7$ tens are $70$, $7$ hundreds are $700$, $7$ thousands are $7\,000$.
To hear a digit's worth, cover everything to its right with your finger and read what the column says.

steps.title: Digit worths
steps.intro: Read the place before the digit.

examples.prompt: What is the $7$ worth in $2\,745$? In $7\,245$?
steps: Thousands column: $7 \times 1\,000 = 7\,000$ — same digit, ten times the worth.

steps.title: Worth spotting
steps.intro: Digit times place, every time.

problems.explanation: The $9$ stands in the hundreds: $9 \times 100 = 900$. Answering $9$ ignores the place; $9\,000$ moves it a column left.
Leftmost of four columns is thousands: $6 \times 1\,000 = 6\,000$.
The $7$ is seven TENS, worth $70$. Add each option back: only $5\,000 + 300 + 70 + 1$ returns $5\,371$.

steps.title: Same digit, three worths
steps.prompt: In $5\,505$ the digit $5$ appears three times. Why are the three worth different amounts?
options: the place gives each its value — $5\,000$, $500$ and $5$
they are all worth the same $5$
the zero between them changes the fives
steps.explanation: Thousands, hundreds and ones columns: $5 \times 1\,000 = 5\,000$, $5 \times 100 = 500$, $5 \times 1 = 5$. Together with the guard on tens duty: $5\,000 + 500 + 5 = 5\,505$.

steps.title: Ten symbols beat a whole alphabet
steps.body: Place value is why you only ever need the ten digits $0$ to $9$: the same $7$ can mean seven, seventy or seven thousand depending on where it stands. Roman numerals had no places, so bigger numbers kept needing new letters — X for ten, C for a hundred, M for a thousand — and arithmetic with them was famously painful.

steps.title: Expanded form, there and back
beats: Expanded form takes a number apart into its worths: $3\,482$ $= 3\,000 + 400 + 80 + 2$. The number line below builds it part by part: jump $3\,000$, then $400$ more to $3\,400$, then $80$ to $3\,480$ — three landings you can see. The last part is a single step of $2$ from $3\,480$ onto $3\,482$, far too small to draw beside a jump of $3\,000$ — which is exactly what place value means.
Building runs backwards: $8\,000 + 40 + 6$ fills the columns as $8$, guard, $4$, $6$ — $8\,046$. A missing part means a zero, never a shorter number.
Always add your parts back. If they return a different number, a part sat in the wrong column.

steps.title: Building from parts
steps.intro: Fill the columns; the guard covers missing parts.

steps: $8\,046$ — the zero holds the hundreds open.

examples.prompt: Build the number with $7$ thousands, $0$ hundreds, $2$ tens and $9$ ones.

steps.title: Parts in, number out
steps.intro: Add the parts; watch for guards.

problems.explanation: No tens part, so a zero guards the tens: $4\,605$. Choosing $4\,650$ pushes the $5$ into the tens, making it $50$.
$2\,000 + 30 + 3 = 2\,033$ — the hundreds column is empty, so its guard steps in.
The $9$ stands in the tens: $6\,000 + 90$. The trap $6\,000 + 900$ builds $6\,900$ instead.

steps.title: The silent column
steps.prompt: A number's expanded form is $9\,000 + 300 + 8$. Its tens digit is:
steps.explanation: No tens part appears, so the tens column is empty and holds the guard: the number is $9\,308$, tens digit $0$.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A digit's worth is digit × place — read the place before the digit.
One column left = worth ten times more.
Expanded form: one part per column, and the parts must add back exactly.
Building from parts: fill the columns; a missing part becomes a zero.
Adding parts back is the receipt that catches wrong columns.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For each answer, add the parts back (or take the number apart) as a receipt — parts and number must agree before you move on.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Worths, parts and receipts.

problems.explanation: Thousands column: $4 \times 1\,000 = 4\,000$.
Zero guards the tens, so there is no tens part: $7\,000 + 600 + 4$. Adding $40$ instead builds $7\,640$.
Every column holds a $5$: $5\,555$ — four fives, four different worths.

problems.prompt: Using each of the digit cards $1, 7, 4, 9$ once, the LARGEST number you can build is:
problems.explanation: Big digits want big places: $9$ in thousands, then $7$, $4$, $1$ — $9\,741$. Smallest would be $1\,479$, the same cards reversed into small places.

problems.prompt: Paying $3\,260$ togrog with $1\,000$ notes, $100$ notes and $10$ coins takes:
problems.explanation: Read the columns: $3$ thousands, $2$ hundreds, $6$ tens — $3 \times 1\,000 + 2 \times 100 + 6 \times 10 = 3\,260$ togrog.

steps.title: You've finished "Place Value"
steps.body: Digit times place, taken apart and rebuilt — expanded form is the receipt behind every number. Next: putting numbers in ORDER, where the leftmost place speaks first and settles almost every argument.

lessons.title: Comparing & Ordering
lessons.concreteComparison: Two herds meet at the well: one of $3\,025$ animals, one of $2\,970$. The second has showier digits — $970$ looks grander than $25$ — but three THOUSANDS beat two thousands before the small columns even get to speak. Comparing numbers is a conversation where the leftmost place talks first, and the rest only matter if it ties.
lessons.objective: Compare four-digit numbers place by place from the left, order sets of three or four numbers, and place a number between its neighbouring hundreds on the number line.
concept: **More digits wins outright.** A four-digit number always beats a three-digit one: $1\,023$ $> 987$, because $987$ never even reaches $1\,000$. Count digits before comparing them.

**Same length: leftmost place speaks first.** Compare thousands, then hundreds, then tens, then ones — and the FIRST difference settles it. $3\,025$ $>$ $2\,970$ because $3 > 2$ in the thousands; the $970$ never gets a vote.

**Every number lives between two hundreds.** $5\,642$ sits between $5\,600$ and $5\,700$ on the number line — $42$ steps past $5\,600$, $58$ short of $5\,700$. Placing a number between its neighbours is how ordering becomes a picture.
lessons.keyIdea: Count digits first, then compare place by place from the left — the first difference decides. On the number line, bigger simply means further right.

facts.title: Leftmost place speaks first
facts.explanation: The first column that differs settles it; later columns cannot overturn it.

facts.title: Between the hundreds
facts.explanation: Every four-digit number sits between two neighbouring hundreds on the line.

workedExamples.statement: Which herd is larger: $3\,025$ animals or $2\,970$?
workedExamples.note: Thousands first — the flashy hundreds never vote.
workedExamples.solution: Both have four digits, so compare thousands: $3 > 2$, done — $3\,025$ $>$ $2\,970$. Even the smaller herd's whole $2\,970$ stays below the bigger herd's $3\,000$ of thousands alone.

workedExamples.note: Walk the columns left to right until they differ.
workedExamples.solution: All share $5$ thousands. Hundreds: $4, 4, 5$ — so $5\,504$ is largest. Between the two with $4$ hundreds, tens decide: $6 < 7$, so $5\,461$ $<$ $5\,470$. Order: $5\,461$ $<$ $5\,470$ $<$ $5\,504$.

commonMistakes.text: Letting a flashy small column decide — 2 895 > 3 014 "because 8 beats 0".
commonMistakes.correction: The hundreds only speak if the thousands TIE. 3 > 2 in the thousands ends the contest: 3 014 is bigger, whatever the later digits.

commonMistakes.text: Comparing first digits across different lengths — 987 > 1 023 "because 9 beats 1".
commonMistakes.correction: Count digits first. Four columns beat three: 987 is below 1 000 and 1 023 is above it, so 1 023 > 987.

tryIt.solution: Thousands tie, hundreds tie; tens: $8 > 4$ — so $6\,384$ $>$ $6\,348$. The difference is $36$: $6\,348 + 36 = 6\,384$.

tryIt.statement: What number sits exactly halfway between $4\,200$ and $4\,300$?

steps.title: The leftmost place speaks first
beats: Count digits before anything else: a four-digit number beats a three-digit one every time — $987 < 1\,023$, because $987$ never reaches $1\,000$.

Same length? Compare column by column from the LEFT: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. The first difference settles it — $3\,025$ beats $2\,970$ because $3 > 2$ in the thousands. The picture below stacks the two numbers column by column: $2\,970$ has the showier hundreds and tens, and still loses on the very first column.
The place gives the digit its value — that is exactly why the left column outvotes everything: one step of a thousand is more than the other three columns can hold together.

steps.title: First difference wins
steps.intro: Digits counted, then columns walked from the left.

steps: Three digits against four: no contest.

steps.title: Column court
steps.intro: First difference from the left decides.

problems.explanation: Thousands and hundreds tie; tens: $1 < 6$ — so $<$. The swapped last digits try to distract; the tens speak before the ones.
Thousands first: $5$ beats $4$, so $5\,001$ wins despite its tiny-looking $001$ tail.
Three digits against four: $999$ is the LAST three-digit number and still loses — $999 + 2 = 1\,001$.

steps.title: Flashy digits do not vote
steps.prompt: A student says $2\,895$ $>$ $3\,014$ "because $8$ beats $0$". The truth:
options: thousands speak first: $3 > 2$, so $3\,014$ is bigger
the student is right — hundreds count more
steps.explanation: Hundreds only get a vote when thousands TIE. Here $3\,000$ alone already beats the whole of $2\,895$ — the later columns cannot catch up.

steps.title: Why the later columns cannot rebel
steps.body: Once the thousands differ, the contest is truly over: the hundreds, tens and ones together can only ever add up to $999$ — one whole step of a thousand is bigger, since $999 < 1\,000$. The leftmost place is not just first, it is unbeatable.

steps.title: Ordering, and the number line
beats: To order three or four numbers, run the same contest repeatedly: find the smallest, then the next — $5\,461$ $<$ $5\,470$ $<$ $5\,504$.
Every number lives BETWEEN two neighbouring hundreds. On the line below, $5\,642$ sits between $5\,600$ and $5\,700$: it is $42$ past $5\,600$ and $58$ short of $5\,700$.
On the number line, bigger simply means further right — ordering numbers is placing them on the line and reading left to right.

steps.title: Between the neighbours
steps.intro: Find the hundreds on each side; measure both gaps.

examples.prompt: Which hundreds does $5\,642$ sit between, and how far from each?

steps: Thousands tie; hundreds put $5\,504$ on top.

steps.title: On the line
steps.intro: Between-ness is a picture — read it left to right.

problems.prompt: The line below shows the gap from $3\,400$ to $3\,500$. Which number lands inside it?
problems.explanation: Only $3\,456$ lands inside the gap: $3\,400 < 3\,456 < 3\,500$. The others fall outside — $3\,390$ is below $3\,400$ and $3\,540$ beyond $3\,500$.
Hundreds first: the $9$-hundreds number $4\,908$ is largest. Then tens: $8 < 9$ puts $4\,089$ before $4\,098$.
Half of the thousand-wide gap is $500$: $6\,000 + 500 = 6\,500$, and $500$ more reaches $7\,000$.

steps.title: Herds in order
steps.prompt: A family counts $2\,041$ sheep, $1\,998$ goats and $1\,899$ horses. From largest herd to smallest:
steps.explanation: Sheep clear $2\,000$; the others stay below it. Between goats and horses the hundreds decide: $9 > 8$, so goats beat horses.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Count digits first: four columns beat three, always.
Same length: compare place by place from the LEFT — first difference decides.
Later columns cannot overturn an earlier difference: they top out at 999.
Every number sits between two neighbouring hundreds; measure both gaps.
On the number line, bigger means further right.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Before each comparison, say which column will speak first — then let it. Ordering is just comparing, repeated.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Contests, orders, and the line.

problems.explanation: Tens speak first here: $1 < 4$, so $<$. The gap is $27$: $8\,514 + 27 = 8\,541$.
Thousands all tie at $9$ — the hundreds decide: $9 > 0$, so $9\,900$ leads. The zeros sit in different columns in each number.
$7\,800 < 7\,856 < 7\,900$. The others miss the gap: $7\,908$ overshoots, $7\,790$ falls short.

problems.prompt: Three Naadam riders cover $4\,320$ m, $4\,230$ m and $4\,302$ m. Ordered shortest ride to longest:
problems.explanation: Hundreds first: $2 < 3$ makes $4\,230$ shortest. Then tens: $0 < 2$ puts $4\,302$ before $4\,320$.
The first four-digit number beats the last three-digit one by exactly $1$: $999 + 1 = 1\,000$. Digit count before digit size.

steps.title: You've finished "Comparing & Ordering"
steps.body: Digit count, then the leftmost difference — and the number line to see it all at once. Next: ROUNDING, where the two neighbouring tens or hundreds you just learned to find become the only two answers allowed.

lessons.title: Rounding
lessons.concreteComparison: The Naadam stadium counted $4\,872$ visitors — but you tell your friend "about $4\,900$". Rounding trades an exact number for a nearby round one that the mouth and the mind can carry. The whole skill is finding a number's two round NEIGHBOURS on the number line and moving to the closer one.
lessons.objective: Round four-digit numbers to the nearest 10 and nearest 100 by comparing the two neighbours on the number line, apply the halfway-rounds-up rule, and use rounding to estimate sums.
concept: **Every number has two round neighbours.** To the nearest $10$, $3\,482$ sits between $3\,480$ and $3\,490$. Measure both gaps — $2$ back, $8$ forward — and move to the closer neighbour: $3\,480$.

**The place you round to picks the neighbours.** Nearest $10$: neighbours are tens. Nearest $100$: neighbours are hundreds — $7\,258$ sits between $7\,200$ and $7\,300$, gaps $58$ and $42$, so it rounds to $7\,300$. Same number, different question, different answer.
**Halfway rounds up.** $645$ is exactly $5$ from both $640$ and $650$ — no closer neighbour exists, so the rule steps in: exactly halfway goes UP, to $650$.
lessons.keyIdea: Rounding is a two-neighbour contest on the number line: find the round number on each side, measure both gaps, move to the closer one — and when the gaps tie, go up.

facts.title: The two neighbours
facts.explanation: Gaps of 2 and 8 — the closer neighbour wins, so 3 482 rounds to 3 480.

facts.title: The halfway rule
facts.explanation: Equal gaps on both sides: the rule sends halfway numbers UP.

workedExamples.note: Find both neighbours; measure both gaps.
workedExamples.solution: Neighbouring tens: $3\,480$ and $3\,490$. Gaps: $3\,482 - 3\,480 = 2$ back, $3\,490 - 3\,482 = 8$ forward. The gap of $2$ wins: $3\,482$ rounds to $3\,480$.

workedExamples.note: Nearest hundred means the neighbours are hundreds.
workedExamples.solution: Neighbouring hundreds: $7\,200$ and $7\,300$. Gaps: $58$ back, $42$ forward — the forward gap is smaller, so $7\,258$ rounds UP to $7\,300$.

commonMistakes.text: Rounding to the wrong place — asked for the nearest 10, answering 3 500 for 3 482.
commonMistakes.correction: Nearest TEN means the neighbours are tens: 3 480 and 3 490. Say which place the question names before hunting neighbours.

commonMistakes.text: Sending halfway numbers down — rounding 645 to 640.
commonMistakes.correction: 645 is exactly 5 from both neighbours; no side is closer. The agreed rule breaks the tie UPWARD: 645 rounds to 650.

tryIt.solution: Neighbours $6\,230$ and $6\,240$; gaps $7$ and $3$. Closer neighbour: $6\,240$.
Neighbours $1\,600$ and $1\,700$; gaps $50$ and $50$ — exactly halfway, so the rule sends it UP: $1\,700$.

steps.title: The two-neighbour contest
beats: Rounding to the nearest $10$: find the ten on each side. On the line below, $3\,482$ stands between $3\,480$ and $3\,490$ — $2$ steps past one, $8$ short of the other.
The closer neighbour wins: $3\,482$ rounds to $3\,480$. Never guess from the digits alone — MEASURE both gaps.
Nearest $100$ plays the same game with hundred-neighbours: the place named in the question picks which neighbours compete. The place gives the digit its value — and the question names the place.

steps.title: Neighbours and gaps
steps.intro: Name the place, find both neighbours, measure both gaps.

steps: The forward gap is smaller — up to $7\,300$.

steps.title: Closer neighbour wins
steps.intro: Measure both gaps before deciding.

problems.explanation: Neighbours $5\,620$ and $5\,630$: gaps $3$ and $7$, so $5\,620$. Answering $5\,600$ rounds to the wrong place — that is the nearest hundred.
Hundred-neighbours $2\,300$ and $2\,400$: gaps $80$ and $20$. The $20$ wins — up to $2\,400$.

problems.prompt: The line shows $8\,361$ between its hundred-neighbours. To the nearest $100$ it rounds to:
problems.explanation: Gaps: $61$ back to $8\,300$, $39$ forward to $8\,400$ — forward is closer. ($8\,360$ answers a nearest-ten question instead.)

steps.title: Just under the middle
steps.explanation: Neighbours $4\,000$ and $4\,100$: gaps $49$ and $51$. One short of halfway — the smaller gap points down to $4\,000$. ($4\,050$ rounds to the nearest ten, a different question.)

steps.title: Rounding never wanders far
steps.body: A rounded number can never drift more than HALF a step from the truth: to the nearest $10$ at most $5$ away, to the nearest $100$ at most $50$. That guarantee is what makes estimates trustworthy — the error is fenced in before you even start.

steps.title: Halfway up, then estimate
beats: Sometimes the contest ties: $645$ is exactly $5$ from $640$ and $5$ from $650$ — the line below shows it dead centre. The agreed rule: exactly halfway rounds UP, so $645$ goes to $650$.
The same rule at hundreds: $450$ sits $50$ from $400$ and $50$ from $500$ — up to $500$.

Rounding earns its keep in ESTIMATES: to check $2\,387 + 4\,615$, round both to hundreds — $2\,400 + 4\,600 = 7\,000$. The exact sum, $7\,002$, lands right beside it: the estimate backs up the answer.

steps.title: Ties and estimates
steps.intro: Halfway goes up; rounded sums forecast exact ones.

steps: Gaps: $5$ to $640$ and $5$ to $650$ — a tie.

examples.prompt: Estimate $2\,387 + 4\,615$ by rounding each to the nearest $100$, then compare with the exact sum.

steps.title: Halfway and beyond
steps.intro: Ties go up; estimates go first.

problems.explanation: Gaps: $50$ to $700$ and $50$ to $800$ — exactly halfway, and halfway rounds UP: $800$.

problems.prompt: Rounding to the nearest $100$, the estimate for $3\,190 + 2\,807$ is:
problems.explanation: Round each number to its own closer neighbour: $3\,190$ is $10$ from $3\,200$, and $2\,807$ is $7$ from $2\,800$. The exact sum $5\,997$ sits $3$ below the estimate. The wrong options round one number the far way and land $100$ off.
Gaps: $50$ to $9\,900$ and $50$ to $10\,000$ — halfway rounds UP, straight to the fifth-column number itself.

steps.title: The estimate as a check
steps.prompt: To check $4\,512 + 3\,498$, a student estimates $4\,500 + 3\,500 = 8\,000$. The exact sum is $8\,010$. The estimate is:
options: $10$ under — close enough to back up the exact answer
$100$ under — the addition must be wrong
useless, because it is not exact
steps.explanation: Each rounding moved at most $50$, so estimate and truth must land near each other: $8\,010 - 8\,000 = 10$. An estimate is a check, not a replacement.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rounding is a two-neighbour contest: find both, measure both gaps, move to the closer.
The question names the place, and the place picks the neighbours — ten-neighbours or hundred-neighbours.
Exactly halfway (gap 5, or gap 50) rounds UP.
Nearest 10 stays within 5 of the truth; nearest 100 within 50.
Round-then-add gives an estimate that backs up the exact sum.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For every rounding below, write BOTH neighbours and both gaps before answering — the wrong-place trap cannot survive that habit.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Neighbours, ties, and estimates.

problems.explanation: Neighbours $2\,760$ and $2\,770$: gaps $4$ and $6$ — down to $2\,760$. ($2\,800$ answers the nearest-hundred question.)
Gaps: $49$ back to $6\,100$, $51$ forward to $6\,200$ — one short of halfway, so DOWN.
Gaps: $5$ and $5$ — halfway rounds UP to $990$. ($1\,000$ would answer a nearest-hundred question.)
Halfway between $1\,400$ and $1\,500$ — gaps of $50$ each — and halfway goes UP.

problems.prompt: A shop sells $2\,480$ tickets in June and $1\,520$ in July. Rounding each to the nearest $100$, the estimated total is:
options: $2\,500 + 1\,500 = 4\,000$ — and the exact total is $4\,000$ too
problems.explanation: Each number is $20$ from its closer neighbour, in opposite directions — the errors cancel and the estimate lands exactly: $2\,480 + 1\,520 = 4\,000$. The wrong options send one number to its FAR neighbour ($2\,480$ down to $2\,400$, or $1\,520$ up to $1\,600$) and miss by $100$.

steps.title: You've finished "Rounding"
steps.body: Two neighbours, a measured gap, and a tie-breaking rule — plus estimates that check your arithmetic. Last stop: number PATTERNS, where the same step repeats and the ones digit tells secrets.

lessons.title: Number Patterns
lessons.concreteComparison: Counting togrog notes into a tin — $100$, $200$, $300$ — your hand finds the rhythm before your head does. A number pattern is exactly that rhythm written down: the SAME step, taken again and again. Name the step and you own the pattern — you can continue it as far as you like.
lessons.objective: Skip count by 25s, 50s and 100s, find a pattern's step by subtracting neighbours, continue and describe patterns, and tell odd from even using the ones digit.
concept: **A pattern's step is found by subtracting.** In $4\,200, 4\,250, 4\,300$ the step is $4\,250 - 4\,200 = 50$ — and every neighbouring pair must agree. To continue, keep adding the step: $4\,350, 4\,400$.
**The favourite steps are 25, 50 and 100.** They fit hundreds perfectly: four 25s or two 50s make $100$, so these counts land on round numbers again and again — $925, 950, 975, 1\,000$.

**Odd or even lives in the ones digit.** A number is EVEN if it splits into two equal teams, and only the ones digit decides: every ten, hundred and thousand already splits evenly, so the leftover ones digit settles it — $3\,482$ ends in $2$: even. $4\,507$ ends in $7$: odd.
lessons.keyIdea: Subtract neighbours to name the step, then add it to continue — and for odd or even, ask only the ones digit: all the bigger places split evenly by themselves.

facts.title: Name the step
facts.explanation: Subtract any neighbouring pair; every pair must give the same step.

facts.title: The ones digit decides
facts.explanation: Tens, hundreds and thousands split into pairs by themselves — only the ones digit can leave one out.

workedExamples.statement: Continue the pattern with two more numbers, and name its step: $4\,200, 4\,250, 4\,300$.
workedExamples.note: Subtract neighbours first — never guess the step.

workedExamples.solution: $3\,482$ ends in $2$ — even: it splits into two equal teams with nobody left over. $4\,507$ ends in $7$ — odd: pairing always leaves one out. The big columns never matter; they split evenly by themselves.

commonMistakes.text: Guessing the step from the loudest changing digit — calling 5 650, 5 700, 5 750 "counting by 100s" because the hundreds digit keeps moving.
commonMistakes.correction: Subtract neighbours: 5 700 − 5 650 = 50. The hundreds digit moves because the 50s keep crossing into it — the step itself is 50.

commonMistakes.text: Judging odd or even by the first digit — "2 467 is even because it starts with 2".
commonMistakes.correction: Only the ONES digit votes: 2 467 ends in 7, so it is odd. The 2 000 and 400 and 60 all split into pairs without help.

tryIt.statement: Continue with one more number and name the step: $6\,100, 6\,200, 6\,300$.

tryIt.solution: $5\,550$ ends in $0$ — even. $5\,505$ ends in $5$ — odd. Same digits, different ones place, different answer.

steps.title: Name the step, own the pattern
beats: A skip-count takes the SAME step again and again. To name the step, SUBTRACT neighbours: in $4\,200, 4\,250, 4\,300$ the step is $50$ — and every pair must agree.
To continue, keep adding: the line below shows the next two landings, $4\,350$ and $4\,400$.
The favourite steps $25$, $50$ and $100$ fit the hundreds column perfectly — four $25$s make $100$ — so these counts land on round numbers again and again.

steps.title: Continue the count
steps.intro: Subtract to name the step; add to continue it.

steps.title: Step detective
steps.intro: Subtract neighbours; never guess.

problems.explanation: Step: $3\,100 - 3\,000 = 100$; so $3\,200 + 100 = 3\,300$. Jumping to $4\,200$ adds a thousand, not a hundred.
$7\,450 - 7\,425 = 25$, and the second pair agrees. The ones and tens digits cycle $25, 50, 75$ — the signature of a $25$ count.
$9\,950 + 50 = 10\,000$ — the count walks right up to the fifth-column number.

steps.title: The loud digit lies
steps.prompt: In $5\,650, 5\,700, 5\,750$ a student names the step $100$, because the hundreds digit keeps changing. The real step:
steps.explanation: Subtraction, not appearances: both gaps are $50$. The hundreds digit moves because each $50$ step keeps crossing a hundred boundary — the loud digit is a side effect, not the step.

steps.title: Why 25 feels so round
steps.body: Counting by $25$s lands on a whole hundred every fourth step — $25, 50, 75, 100$ — because $4 \times 25 = 100$. Keep going and every landing stays friendly: forty steps of $25$ reach exactly $1\,000$. That perfect fit is why coins and scores the world over love quarters of a hundred.

steps.title: Odd and even — ask the ones digit
beats: A number is EVEN when it splits into two equal teams with nobody left over: $8$ children make teams of $4$ and $4$, as the picture shows. ODD numbers always leave one out.

For big numbers you never need to split anything: every ten, hundred and thousand splits evenly by itself, so only the ONES digit can leave someone out. Ending $0, 2, 4, 6, 8$: even. Ending $1, 3, 5, 7, 9$: odd.
So $3\,482$ is even (ends in $2$) and $4\,507$ is odd (ends in $7$) — verdicts read straight off the last digit.

steps.title: Even splits
steps.intro: The ones digit gives the verdict; a fair split is the receipt.

steps: $3\,482$ even; $4\,507$ odd — the big columns never vote.

examples.prompt: Can $746$ sheep be split into two equal flocks?

steps.title: Odd one out
steps.intro: Last digit only — the rest is noise.

problems.explanation: Ones digits $5, 4, 8$: only the $5$ is odd. The shared $2\,43$ start is identical noise.
Only the ones digit votes: $1$ is odd, so $6\,001$ is odd — even though $6\,000$ right beside it is even.
The bigger places always split evenly, so the ones digit is the whole test — $3\,480$ is even, $3\,485$ is odd, and only the last digit changed the verdict.

steps.title: The first digit has no vote
steps.prompt: A student calls $2\,467$ even "because it starts with $2$". The truth:
options: odd — only the ones digit votes, and $7$ is odd
even — more of its digits are even than odd
it depends on the number before it
steps.explanation: The $2\,460$ part splits into pairs perfectly — it is even on its own — so everything hangs on the final $7$, which leaves one out: odd.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Name a pattern's step by SUBTRACTING neighbours — every pair must agree.
Continue by adding the step; describe the pattern by its step, not its digits.
25, 50 and 100 fit the hundreds perfectly — their counts keep landing on round numbers.
Even splits into two equal teams; odd leaves one out.
Only the ones digit decides odd or even — the bigger places split evenly by themselves.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For each pattern below, write the step above every gap before continuing — and for each odd-or-even, point at the ones digit and ignore the rest.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Steps, continuations, and verdicts.

problems.explanation: Step: $2\,000 - 1\,975 = 25$; so $2\,025 + 25 = 2\,050$. The count strides across the thousand boundary without stumbling.
Ones digits: $9$ (odd) and $0$ (even). Neighbouring numbers ALWAYS disagree — odd and even alternate forever.

problems.prompt: Ticket sales climb by $100$s: $4\,700, 4\,800, 4\,900$, and then:
problems.explanation: Step $100$: $4\,900 + 100 = 5\,000$ — the count rolls the thousands column over.

problems.prompt: Which number BREAKS the by-$25$ pattern $4\,025, 4\,050, 4\,075, 4\,090$?
problems.explanation: The first gaps are $25$ and $25$, but $4\,090 - 4\,075 = 15$ — the wrong step. The true next landing is $4\,100$.

steps.title: You've finished "Number Patterns" — and the topic
steps.body: Columns and their names, digit times place, the leftmost contest, the two-neighbour round, and steps that repeat: the whole world below ten thousand, mapped. Next year the same place-value ideas stretch to numbers in the millions — the columns just keep going left.

practice.statement: Write "eight thousand and forty" as a numeral.
practice.solution: Thousands $8$, hundreds empty, tens $4$, ones empty — two zero guards: $8\,040$.

practice.statement: What is the $5$ worth in $5\,213$? And in $2\,513$?
practice.solution: In $5\,213$ it stands in the thousands: $5 \times 1\,000 = 5\,000$. In $2\,513$ it stands in the hundreds: $5 \times 100 = 500$ — one column right, one tenth the worth.
$9\,000 + 300 + 6$ — the tens column is empty, so no tens part appears. Receipt: the parts add back to $9\,306$.
Thousands tie at $6$. Hundreds: $1 < 5$ makes $6\,125$ smallest. Between the two with $5$ hundreds, tens decide: $1 < 2$, so $6\,512$ $<$ $6\,521$. Order: $6\,125$ $<$ $6\,512$ $<$ $6\,521$.

practice.statement: The line shows $2\,764$ between its neighbouring hundreds. How far is it from each of them, and what does $2\,764$ round to at the nearest $100$?
practice.solution: Gaps: $2\,764 - 2\,700 = 64$ past $2\,700$, and $2\,800 - 2\,764 = 36$ short of $2\,800$. The smaller gap wins, so to the nearest $100$, $2\,764$ rounds to $2\,800$.

practice.statement: Round $4\,385$ to the nearest $10$, and then to the nearest $100$.
practice.solution: Nearest $10$: neighbours $4\,380$ and $4\,390$, gaps $5$ and $5$ — halfway rounds UP to $4\,390$. Nearest $100$: neighbours $4\,300$ and $4\,400$, gaps $85$ and $15$ — the $15$ wins: $4\,400$.

practice.statement: Estimate $3\,245 + 2\,178$ by rounding each to the nearest $100$, then find the exact sum.
practice.solution: Round: $3\,200 + 2\,200 = 5\,400$. Exact: $3\,245 + 2\,178 = 5\,423$ — the estimate sits $23$ below, close enough to back it up.

practice.statement: Continue $8\,500, 8\,550, 8\,600$ with two more numbers. Is your first new number odd or even?

testYourself.statement: Write "seven thousand and six" as a numeral, and $3\,090$ in words.
testYourself.solution: Seven thousand and six: thousands $7$, then two zero guards, then $6$ — $7\,006$. And $3\,090$ reads "three thousand and ninety": the guard silences the hundreds.

testYourself.statement: What is the $8$ worth in $8\,245$, and in $2\,845$? Write $8\,245$ in expanded form.

testYourself.solution: Thousands all tie. Hundreds split the field: the $0$-hundreds pair comes first, the $8$-hundreds pair second. Tens finish it: $4\,078$ $<$ $4\,087$ $<$ $4\,807$ $<$ $4\,870$.
$6\,550$: gaps of $50$ to each neighbour — exactly halfway, so UP to $6\,600$. $6\,549$: gaps $49$ down, $51$ up — one below halfway, so DOWN to $6\,500$. One apart, they round apart.

testYourself.statement: A school orders $1\,890$ red caps and $2\,130$ blue caps. Estimate the total by rounding each to the nearest $100$, then find the exact total.
testYourself.solution: Round: $1\,900 + 2\,100 = 4\,000$. Exact: $1\,890 + 2\,130 = 4\,020$ — the estimate lands $20$ under, backing up the sum.

testYourself.statement: Continue $2\,925, 2\,950, 2\,975$ with two more numbers, name the step, and say which of your two new numbers is even.
